claim: All three brain regions (anterior PFC, lateral PFC, and STN) demonstrated significant decreases in beta band (15–30 Hz) power across all trials (p < 0.005, permutation test).
source: Across sessions, all three brain regions demonstrated significant decreases in beta band (15–30 Hz) power across all trials (p < 0.005, permutation test; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of oscillatory power changes with p-values.

claim: Significant increases in theta band (2–8 Hz) power were found in the anterior and lateral PFC during the task (p < 0.005 for anterior PFC and lateral PFC, permutation test).
source: We also found significant increases in theta band (2–8 Hz) power in the anterior and lateral PFC during the task (p < 0.005 for anterior PFC and lateral PFC, permutation test, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of theta power changes with p-values.

claim: During the distractor trials, both the STN and lateral PFC demonstrated an early termination of the beta band decrease, resulting in significantly higher beta band power relative to the target trials (p = 0.020 for STN and p = 0.025 for lateral PFC, permutation test).
source: However, during the distractor trials, both the STN and lateral PFC demonstrated an early termination of the beta band decrease. This resulted in significantly higher beta band power relative to the target trials (p = 0.020 for STN and p = 0.025 for lateral PFC, permutation test; Figure 3; see Materials and methods; for changes in theta band power, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison between trial types with p-values.

claim: In 19 out of the 24 sessions with lateral PFC electrodes, at least one electrode contact exhibited a significant decrease in beta power during the task (p < 0.05, permutation test).
source: In 19 out of the 24 sessions with lateral PFC electrodes, at least one electrode contact exhibited a significant decrease in beta power during the task (p < 0.05, permutation test; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of sessions showing significant effects with statistical testing.

claim: 14 out of 29 sessions with anterior PFC electrodes demonstrated at least one electrode contact exhibiting a significant decrease in beta power during the task (p < 0.05, permutation test).
source: In contrast, 14 out of 29 sessions with anterior PFC electrodes demonstrated at least one electrode contact exhibiting a significant decrease in beta power during the task (p < 0.05, permutation test).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of sessions showing significant effects with statistical testing.

claim: 13 out of the 24 experimental sessions with lateral PFC electrodes demonstrated a significant difference between target and distractor trials in at least one contact (p < 0.05, permutation test).
source: We found that 13 out of the 24 experimental sessions with lateral PFC electrodes demonstrated a significant difference between target and distractor trials in at least one contact (p < 0.05, permutation test).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of sessions showing significant trial-type differences.

claim: In the anterior PFC, only 6 out of 29 sessions demonstrated at least one contact exhibiting a significant difference in average beta power between target and distractor trials (p < 0.05, permutation test).
source: Conversely, in the anterior PFC, only 6 out of 29 sessions demonstrated at least one contact exhibiting a significant difference in average beta power between target and distractor trials (p < 0.05, permutation test).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of sessions showing significant trial-type differences.

claim: In the lateral PFC electrodes, successfully encoded target trials exhibited significantly greater decreases in beta power than those target trials that participants failed to encode (p = 0.04, permutation test).
source: In the lateral PFC electrodes, we found that the successfully encoded target trials exhibited significantly greater decreases in beta power than those target trials that participants failed to encode (p = 0.04, permutation test; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison between correct and error trials with p-values.

claim: No similar differences between error trials and successfully encoded target trials were found in the anterior PFC (p = 0.17, permutation test) or the STN (p = 0.20, permutation test).
source: We did not, however, find similar differences between the error trials and the successfully encoded target trials in the anterior PFC (p = 0.17, permutation test) or the STN (p = 0.20, permutation test, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons showing no significant differences with p-values.

claim: Distractor trials exhibited significantly higher coherence in the beta band between the lateral PFC and the STN than target trials (p = 0.015, permutation procedure).
source: Distractor trials exhibited significantly higher coherence in the beta band between the lateral PFC and the STN than target trials (p = 0.015, permutation procedure; Figure 4), suggesting that the elevated levels of beta power in both brain regions during distractor trials were accompanied by elevated levels of beta band coherence.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of coherence between trial types with p-values.

claim: The increased coherence observed during distractor trials was primarily driven by higher levels of phase synchrony (p = 0.025, permutation test).
source: The increased coherence we observed during distractor trials was primarily driven by higher levels of phase synchrony (p = 0.025, permutation test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of phase synchrony with p-values.

claim: On average, across all neurons, there was a significant decrease in overall spiking activity during each trial compared to baseline (p = 0.02, permutation test).
source: On average, across all neurons, we found a significant decrease in overall spiking activity during each trial compared to baseline (p = 0.02, permutation test; see Materials and methods; Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of spiking activity with p-values.

claim: 47.9% (23 out of 48 clusters) of the recorded clusters demonstrated a significant change in firing rate (p < 0.05, permutation test) during the task when compared to baseline.
source: Within individual recordings, we found that 47.9% (23 out of 48 clusters) of the recorded clusters demonstrated a significant change in firing rate (p < 0.05, permutation test) during the task (across all trials) when compared to baseline (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons showing significant changes with statistical testing.

claim: Of the neuronal clusters that showed a change in firing, 65% (15 out of 23 clusters) exhibited significant decreases in firing during the task, while 35% (8 out of 23 clusters) exhibited significant increases.
source: Of these neuronal clusters that showed a change in firing, most (65%, 15 out of 23 clusters) exhibited significant decreases in firing during the task, but some (35%, 8 out of 23 clusters) exhibited significant increases (average responses of both populations in Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data on the proportion of neurons showing different response types.

claim: Neuronal clusters exhibiting decreased spiking activity were significantly entrained to ongoing beta oscillations during the task (p = 0.02, permutation test).
source: Nevertheless, we examined the relationship between individual spike events and the ongoing LFP oscillations recorded from the STN macroelectrodes, and found that these neuronal clusters were significantly entrained to ongoing beta oscillations during the task (p = 0.02, permutation test; Figure 5F; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of spike-phase locking with p-values.

claim: The neuronal clusters that individually demonstrated increases in spiking activity during the task did not exhibit a significant interaction between LFP phase and spiking events (p = 0.16, permutation test).
source: Notably, the neuronal clusters that individually demonstrated increases in spiking activity during the task did not exhibit a significant interaction between LFP phase and spiking events (p = 0.16, permutation test; Figure 5F).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing no significant spike-phase locking with p-values.

claim: Individual recordings accounting for approximately 20% of the recorded neuronal clusters exhibited significant differences in spiking activity between target and distractor trials (p < 0.05, permutation test).
source: Individual recordings accounting for approximately 20% of the recorded neuronal clusters exhibited significant differences in spiking activity between target and distractor trials (p < 0.05, permutation test; Figure 5G).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons showing trial-type differences with statistical testing.

claim: There were no significant overall differences in spiking activity between target and distractor trials across either decreasing neurons (p = 0.34, permutation test) or increasing neurons (p = 0.36, permutation test).
source: However, we found no significant overall differences in spiking activity between target and distractor trials across either decreasing (p = 0.34, permutation test; Figure 5H) or increasing neurons (p = 0.36, permutation test).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons showing no significant differences with p-values.

claim: The basal ganglia have traditionally been implicated in facilitating or inhibiting motor movements.
source: The basal ganglia have traditionally been implicated in facilitating or inhibiting motor movements (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature to support this established view.

claim: Studies tying the basal ganglia to decision making have focused on decisions in which participants either make or withhold a motor command.
source: As such, studies tying the basal ganglia to decision making have focused on decisions in which participants either make or withhold a motor command (Zavala et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature to characterize the focus of previous research.

claim: Most studies of working memory have implicated several regions in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in regulating whether and how memories are successfully encoded.
source: Most studies of working memory have implicated several regions in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in regulating whether and how memories are successfully encoded (McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Spitzer et al., 2010; Voytek and Knight, 2010; Heinrichs-Graham and Wilson, 2015; Wiesman et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies to support this established finding.

claim: The decision to execute or withhold a movement involves a race between competing basal ganglia pathways that facilitate or inhibit motor commands.
source: The decision to execute or withhold a movement involves a race between competing basal ganglia pathways that facilitate or inhibit motor commands (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature to support this mechanistic model.

claim: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) has been previously implicated in motor decisions.
source: At the center of this race lies the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a structure within the basal ganglia previously implicated in motor decisions (Kühn et al., 2004; Frank et al., 2007; Cavanagh et al., 2011; Zaghloul et al., 2012; Alegre et al., 2013; Zavala et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies to support the STN's role in motor decisions.

claim: The basal ganglia exhibit extensive connections with regions of the PFC that have been implicated in working memory.
source: In addition, the basal ganglia exhibit extensive connections with regions of the PFC that have been implicated in working memory (Alexander et al., 1986; Nakano et al., 2000; Chudasama et al., 2003), and imaging studies reveal increased basal ganglia activity during tasks that involve working memory (Chang et al., 2007; McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Murty et al., 2011; Chatham et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior anatomical and imaging studies to support this connectivity.

claim: Imaging studies reveal increased basal ganglia activity during tasks that involve working memory.
source: In addition, the basal ganglia exhibit extensive connections with regions of the PFC that have been implicated in working memory (Alexander et al., 1986; Nakano et al., 2000; Chudasama et al., 2003), and imaging studies reveal increased basal ganglia activity during tasks that involve working memory (Chang et al., 2007; McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Murty et al., 2011; Chatham et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple imaging studies to support this finding.

claim: Patients with Parkinson's disease have disruptions of normal basal ganglia circuitry.
source: Empiric support for the basal ganglia's role in gating memory also arises from studies of patients with Parkinson's disease who have disruptions of normal basal ganglia circuitry (Hammond et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature to support this pathophysiological characteristic.

claim: Patients with Parkinson's disease often experience working memory deficits that correlate with the degree of motor and executive function impairment.
source: These patients often experience working memory deficits that correlate with the degree of motor and executive function impairment (Owen et al., 1997; Lewis et al., 2003; Moustafa et al., 2008; Chiaravalloti et al., 2014; Trujillo et al., 2015; Wiesman et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies to support this clinical observation.

claim: Studies examining whether DBS improves or worsens working memory have not been conclusive.
source: Moreover, patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS), in which high-frequency electrical stimulation is delivered directly to the STN, may experience changes in working memory performance, although studies examining whether DBS improves or worsens working memory have not been conclusive (Hälbig et al., 2004; Hershey et al., 2008; Mayer et al., 2016; Ventre-Dominey et al., 2014; Mollion et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies to characterize the inconsistent findings in the literature.

claim: The human STN modulates both oscillatory and spiking activity as participants make decisions regarding whether to attend to and remember individual items.
source: Our data demonstrate that the human STN modulates both oscillatory and spiking activity as participants make decisions regarding whether to attend to and remember individual items.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding based on the data presented.

claim: The observed differences in neural activity suggest that participants are able to successfully make an internal distinction between the two trial types.
source: Although our data cannot distinguish these possibilities, the observed differences in neural activity suggest that participants are able to successfully make an internal distinction between the two trial types.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the observed neural differences between trial types.

claim: Changes in STN beta oscillatory power have been extensively studied in the context of movement, decreasing during the execution of a movement, and increasing when a movement is inhibited.
source: The most robust changes we observed during our task in both the STN and in the lateral PFC were related to beta oscillatory activity. Changes in STN beta oscillatory power have been extensively studied in the context of movement, decreasing during the execution of a movement, and increasing when a movement is inhibited.
evidence: The manuscript draws on established knowledge from prior research on beta oscillations and movement.

claim: The relation between beta oscillatory activity and movement is most evident during stop inhibition tasks when participants are asked to specifically begin or stop a motor movement.
source: The relation between beta oscillatory activity and movement is most evident during stop inhibition tasks when participants are asked to specifically begin or stop a motor movement (Kühn et al., 2004; Ray et al., 2012; Alegre et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this characterization of beta oscillations in motor tasks.

claim: The timing of beta power differences between trial types is similar between our task and the tasks that required an inhibition of an actual movement, suggesting that the changes observed here are analogous to the previously identified stop signal.
source: Nevertheless, we find that the timing of beta power differences between trial types is similar between our task and the tasks that required an inhibition of an actual movement, suggesting that the changes observed here are analogous to the previously identified stop signal (Kühn et al., 2004; Ray et al., 2012; Alegre et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript infers this analogy by comparing the timing of effects to prior studies.

claim: In stop inhibition tasks, differences in beta power can still alter the behavior of the failed stop trials even when occurring after the erroneous response has already begun.
source: Moreover, in stop inhibition tasks, differences in beta power can still alter the behavior of the failed stop trials (in which a subject failed to properly inhibit an action) even when occurring after the erroneous response has already begun. These differences in beta power persist after that behavior has been initiated, and in the case of movement inhibition, this manifests itself as a suppression of the effort and duration of an erroneous response (Ruiz et al., 2011; Cohen and van Gaal, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this observation about beta power and behavior.

claim: Beta band activity may represent the brain's mechanism for globally suppressing all actions.
source: Given the relative timing of the observed changes in beta power and the behavioral and physiological evidence that participants are able to successfully distinguish trial types, our data are therefore consistent with previous studies suggesting that beta band activity may in fact represent the brain's mechanism for globally suppressing all actions.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the data in the context of prior theoretical frameworks.

claim: The concept of global suppression has been well described in the context of movement, but more recently has been extended to include even non-motor processes such as working memory.
source: The concept of global suppression has been well described in the context of movement, but more recently has been extended to include even non-motor processes such as working memory (Wessel et al., 2016a).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature to support this extension of the global suppression concept.

claim: Increases in STN beta oscillatory power have been observed when participants actively refrain from updating working memory.
source: Increases in STN beta oscillatory power have been observed when participants actively refrain from updating working memory (Oswal et al., 2012), and following the presentation of a surprise auditory stimulus that impaired the maintenance of items in working memory (Wessel et al., 2016b).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this observation about beta power and working memory.

claim: Inhibiting movements can result in an unintentional inhibition of memory, suggesting that the suppression of actions related to movement and to memory may be linked.
source: Moreover, inhibiting movements can result in an unintentional inhibition of memory (Chiu and Egner, 2015), suggesting that the suppression of actions related to movement and to memory may be linked.
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study and infers a link between motor and memory suppression.

claim: Beta oscillations in the lateral PFC decrease during the encoding phase of working memory.
source: In particular, beta oscillations in the lateral PFC decrease during the encoding phase of working memory (Spitzer et al., 2010; Brookes et al., 2011; Heinrichs-Graham and Wilson, 2015; Kornblith et al., 2016; Lundqvist et al., 2016; Wiesman et al., 2016), and exhibit similar changes as found in the STN when movements are inhibited (Swann et al., 2009, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple prior studies to support this observation about lateral PFC beta oscillations.

claim: In patients with Parkinson's disease, excessive beta oscillatory activity may not only impact movement, but could also play a role in the observed deficits in working memory due to the global nature of this activity.
source: In patients with Parkinson's disease, therefore, excessive beta oscillatory activity may not only impact movement, but could also play a role in the observed deficits in working memory due to the global nature of this activity (Owen et al., 1997; Lewis et al., 2003; Chiaravalloti et al., 2014; Trujillo et al., 2015; Wiesman et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript infers this possibility based on the data and cites prior studies on working memory deficits in PD.

claim: The effects of excessive beta oscillatory activity on working memory may be related to the loss of dopaminergic innervation to the lateral PFC that result in increased beta oscillations.
source: These effects may be related to the loss of dopaminergic innervation to the lateral PFC that result in increased beta oscillations (Puig and Miller, 2012; Puig et al., 2014; Puig and Miller, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this mechanistic hypothesis.

claim: The changes in beta oscillatory power are accompanied by significant changes in beta oscillatory coherence between the lateral PFC and the STN.
source: Importantly, here we demonstrate that the changes in beta oscillatory power are accompanied by significant changes in beta oscillatory coherence between the lateral PFC and the STN.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a key finding from the coherence analysis.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated progressive increases in gamma band power in the PFC and hippocampus with working memory load.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated progressive increases in gamma band power in the PFC and hippocampus with working memory load (van Vugt et al., 2010; Roux et al., 2012), and in alpha band power in the parietal lobe (Tuladhar et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to provide context for the progressive changes observed.

claim: Progressive decreases in oscillatory activity with working memory load have also been observed across several cortical regions.
source: These progressive changes are not consistent, however, as progressive decreases in oscillatory activity with working memory load have also been observed across several cortical regions (Meltzer et al., 2007), similar to our data.
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study showing similar progressive decreases.

claim: The firing rates of a significant fraction of individual neurons within the STN were modulated during this working memory task that did not involve an explicit motor movement.
source: Our data demonstrate that the firing rates of a significant fraction of individual neurons within the STN were also modulated during this working memory task that did not involve an explicit motor movement.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the spiking activity findings.

claim: Overall firing rates averaged across all neurons decreased during each trial, consistent with the suggestion that decreases in overall STN spiking activity are facilitatory.
source: Overall firing rates averaged across all neurons decreased during each trial, consistent with the suggestion that decreases in overall STN spiking activity are facilitatory.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the spiking data in the context of STN function.

claim: Movement elicits variability in the spiking responses of individual neurons.
source: However, just as movement elicits variability in the spiking responses of individual neurons (Zavala et al., 2017), the decision to attend to and encode items was accompanied by heterogeneous spiking responses.
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study to provide context for the heterogeneous responses observed.

claim: Neurons exhibiting decreased spiking activity also exhibited significant phase locking to the ongoing beta oscillations, suggesting a link between spiking activity in the STN and LFP oscillations.
source: Interestingly, these neurons also exhibited significant phase locking to the ongoing beta oscillations, suggesting a link between spiking activity in the STN and LFP oscillations.
evidence: The manuscript infers this link from the spike-phase locking analysis.

claim: While oscillatory data would implicate the basal ganglia at large in non-motor decisions that distinguish target and distractor items, the spiking data would suggest that only a subset of STN neurons are involved in this process.
source: Hence, while our oscillatory data would implicate the basal ganglia at large in such non-motor decisions that distinguish target and distractor items, the spiking data would suggest that only a subset of STN neurons are involved in this process, and that these neurons do not alter the extent to which they are locked to the ongoing beta oscillations accordingly.
evidence: The manuscript infers this interpretation by contrasting the oscillatory and spiking findings.

claim: The elevated levels of cortical theta oscillatory power during the distractor trials are consistent with the role cortical theta oscillations may play during conflict related response inhibition.
source: The elevated levels of cortical theta oscillatory power during the distractor trials are consistent with the role cortical theta oscillations may play during conflict related response inhibition (Cavanagh et al., 2011, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to interpret the theta power findings.

claim: STN theta increases may be specific to conflict induced slowing of response times rather than complete response inhibition.
source: One possibility, however, is that STN theta increases are specific to conflict induced slowing of response times rather than complete response inhibition.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on a possible explanation for the lack of STN theta differences.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that motor response inhibition as tested using Go-NoGo paradigms fails to elicit differences in theta oscillatory activity despite showing robust changes in the beta band power.
source: Indeed, previous studies have demonstrated that motor response inhibition as tested using Go-NoGo paradigms fails to elicit differences in theta oscillatory activity despite showing robust changes in the beta band power similar to those reported here (Kühn et al., 2004; Ray et al., 2012; Alegre et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this observation about theta oscillations in Go-NoGo tasks.

claim: Many of the circuit mechanisms of the basal ganglia that have been previously described in the context of movement are used in an analogous fashion during non-motor cognitive decisions.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that many of the circuit mechanisms of the basal ganglia that have been previously described in the context of movement are used in an analogous fashion during non-motor cognitive decisions.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: Similar neural mechanisms and interactions between the basal ganglia and the cortex could be used for any non-motor decision that involves proceeding with or aborting a cognitive process.
source: Our data raise the possibility, however, that similar neural mechanisms and interactions between the basal ganglia and the cortex could be used for any non-motor decision that involves proceeding with or aborting a cognitive process.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on broader implications of the findings.

claim: Theta band power was significantly higher during the distractor trials in the anterior and lateral PFC (p = 0.03 for anterior PFC and p = 0.04 for lateral PFC, permutation test) but not in the STN.
source: Theta band power was significantly higher during the distractor trials in the anterior and lateral PFC (p = 0.03 for anterior PFC and p = 0.04 for lateral PFC, permutation test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) but not in the STN.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of theta power between trial types with p-values.

claim: Beta decreases during all encoding trials in the STN and PFC were progressively enhanced as more items were stored into working memory.
source: During all encoding trials, beta band (15–30 Hz) activity decreased in the STN and PFC, and this decrease was progressively enhanced as more items were stored into working memory.
evidence: The abstract summarizes a key finding about progressive beta decreases.

claim: The STN and lateral PFC beta decrease was significantly attenuated during the trials in which participants were instructed not to encode the presented stimulus.
source: Crucially, the STN and lateral PFC beta decrease was significantly attenuated during the trials in which participants were instructed not to encode the presented stimulus.
evidence: The abstract summarizes a key finding about trial-type differences in beta power.

claim: These changes in beta power were associated with increased lateral PFC-STN coherence and altered STN neuronal spiking.
source: These changes were associated with increase lateral PFC-STN coherence and altered STN neuronal spiking.
evidence: The abstract summarizes key findings about coherence and spiking.

claim: The results shed light on why states of altered basal ganglia activity disrupt both motor function and cognition.
source: Our results shed light on why states of altered basal ganglia activity disrupt both motor function and cognition.
evidence: The abstract states the broader implication of the findings.
